brief: A tool caddy with a carry handle and divided bins for screws and bits.

requirements.evidence: Three base pieces joined in a triangle (piece:0,0,0, piece:0,-1,0, piece:-1,0,0), with 12 end caps on the open sides and the joints bolted together
handle:0,0,0;top, fixed to cover:0,0,0;full;top on the middle piece. The configurator checks fit only; whether it can carry a loaded caddy depends on your material and print settings.
bin:0,-1,0~hex-bin-full-div3 (full depth, 3 compartments), holding piles of screws, nuts and standoffs
bin:-1,0,0~hex-bin-full-div2 (full depth, 2 compartments), holding a pile of screws and a pile of standoffs. There's no prop for driver bits, so it isn't shown holding bits.

finish.summary: I built a three-cell tool caddy, and the configurator's checks found no rule errors and no mesh clashes. Two of the cells hold divided bins. The third has a top cover with a carry handle. The configurator only checks how the parts fit. It can't tell whether the handle and joints are strong enough to carry a full caddy: that depends on the plastic and print settings you choose. The open sides of the base pieces are closed with 12 end caps, and the joints between the cells are bolted. That comes to 28 parts, about 1575 g of filament and about 2244 minutes (roughly 37 hours) of printing. For show, I put piles of screws, nuts and standoffs in all five compartments. They sit below the bin rims, so you see them from above, not from the side. There's no prop for driver bits, so the bits compartment holds a pile of standoffs instead.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
